title: Marriage Deserts: Mapping America's Family Divide | Institute for Family Studies
gist: An IFS report uses 2020 Census data at the PUMA level to map US 'marriage deserts' and 'married-family deserts' (places where marriage or married parenthood is rare) and their opposite, 'gardens'. Deserts cluster in urban cores such as Manhattan/Brooklyn, the Bronx and the Mississippi Delta, while gardens are in affluent suburbs such as Dallas-Fort Worth, Northern Virginia and Utah. The gap is 60-70 percentage points, and gardens have about twice the share of households with children.

insights.claim: The Institute for Family Studies defines 'marriage deserts' as PUMAs where fewer than 33% of householders aged 15-64 are married (about the 10th percentile) and 'marriage gardens' as those where at least 61% are married, using 2020 Census data.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: This gives a fine-grained geographic measure of family structure that can be layered onto housing, school and consumer-demand analysis.
insights.quote: marriage deserts are defined as PUMAs in which the share of householders ages 15 to 64 who are married falls below 33% (the rounded 10th percentile for this metric)

insights.claim: The IFS report defines 'married-family deserts' as PUMAs where fewer than 52% of households with children are headed by a married couple, and 'married-family gardens' as those where at least 79% are.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: This measure tracks children's household stability, which is a leading indicator of local human capital.

insights.claim: Harvard economist Raj Chetty's research found that the share of two-parent households is the strongest predictor of upward mobility in a community.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Local family structure is a proxy for long-run economic mobility and the quality of the local labor pool.
insights.quote: the most predictive factor of upward mobility in a community was the share of homes with two parents present in the household

insights.claim: The 'marriage desert' concept is modeled on food deserts: just as healthy groceries are harder to buy in a food desert, entering a stable marriage is likely harder where few people around you are married.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: The idea that family norms spread through neighborhoods implies that local family structure tends to persist over time.
insights.quote: Just as it is harder to buy healthier groceries in a “food desert,” it is likely more difficult to enter into stable married families in a “marriage desert.”

insights.claim: The IFS marriage-deserts report is explicitly descriptive and does not claim causal links between marriage rates, family structure and economic outcomes.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: The maps should be treated as correlational screens, not causal evidence.
insights.quote: this report does not seek to establish causal relationships between marriage rates, family structure, and economic or social outcomes

insights.claim: In the 10 US PUMAs with the lowest marriage shares, only 13% to 17% of householders aged 15-64 are married, compared with 74% to 79% in the top 10 marriage gardens, a spread of more than 60 percentage points.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: US family structure is polarized geographically, with some neighborhoods where marriage is the norm and others where it is rare.

insights.claim: In the top 10 US married-family deserts, only 18% to 26% of households with children are headed by married couples, compared with 86% to 89% in the top 10 married-family gardens, a gap of roughly 70 percentage points.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Children's household stability differs sharply by neighborhood, which affects demand for schools and social services.
insights.quote: in the top married-family deserts, only around 18% to 26% of households with children are headed by married couples

insights.claim: The IFS report argues that the gap between top US marriage deserts and gardens reflects two distinct family-formation regimes rather than variation around one national norm, which it calls 'family structure polarization.'
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: National averages hide two very different local markets for family-related goods, housing and services.
insights.quote: This does not appear to describe small variations around shared national norms, but rather two distinct family-formation regimes

insights.claim: Three Ohio PUMAs (Cleveland, Columbus and Cincinnati) are among the 10 lowest-marriage areas in the US and none are in the top 10 highest, making Ohio a negative outlier; Texas has three of the top 10 marriage gardens and no top-10 deserts.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: This points to possible post-industrial family decline in Ohio compared with family-friendly growth in Texas, which matters for regional demographic forecasts.
insights.quote: Ohio stands out as a negative outlier.

insights.claim: US marriage gardens are mostly suburban and exurban, while marriage deserts are concentrated in city centers, often within the same metro area.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Married families sort into suburbs, which supports suburban single-family housing demand and leaves urban cores more oriented toward adults.
insights.quote: the geography of marriage gardens is overwhelmingly suburban and exurban in character, standing in clear contrast to the urban-core concentration observed among marriage deserts

themes.theme: Largest clusters: NYC deserts vs suburban gardens

insights.claim: The largest contiguous marriage desert in the US covers Lower Manhattan and Brooklyn, with 686,520 householders aged 15-64, and New York's two largest deserts together hold over 1.2 million householders.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: New York's core is a large market dominated by single adults, which shapes housing type (smaller units), retail and services demand.

insights.claim: The largest contiguous marriage garden in the US is suburban Dallas-Fort Worth, with 636,086 householders aged 15-64.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Dallas-Fort Worth suburbs are the largest concentration of married households, which supports family-oriented housing, schools and retail there.
insights.quote: The Suburban Dallas-Fort Worth marriage garden is the largest grouped marriage garden in the country.

insights.claim: The largest contiguous married-family desert in the US is in the Bronx and Manhattan, with 178,144 households with children, while the largest married-family garden runs from the DC suburbs to the Philadelphia suburbs with about 386,000 households with children.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Very different family environments sit within the same Northeast corridor labor and housing markets.

insights.claim: The IFS report argues that New York, the center of American cultural, media and corporate leadership, is a place where low marriage rates are broadly normal, and that its executives likely live in nearby marriage gardens, creating a divide between 'family-haves' and 'family-have-nots.'
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Elite cultural producers working in low-marriage environments may shape media narratives about family in ways that differ from how most families live.
insights.quote: there is a clear divide between the family-haves and the family-have-nots that likely mirrors other forms of inequality in the region

insights.claim: The Mississippi Delta, spanning parts of Louisiana, Mississippi, Arkansas and Tennessee, is the second-largest married-family desert in the US, with 155,492 households with children and married-couple shares of 27% to 52%.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Married-family deserts are not only urban; large rural regions show the same pattern, with implications for demand for public services.

insights.claim: California, Illinois, Maryland, New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania each have both top-10 married-family gardens and top-10 married-family deserts, which makes them arguably the most divided US states for family experience.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Family-structure inequality within these states may affect state politics and how state budgets are allocated.
insights.quote: making them arguably the most divided states in America for family experience

insights.claim: Large US married-family gardens are often in affluent, institutionally influential regions with limited housing, such as Northern Virginia, the San Francisco Bay Area and parts of Connecticut, which is consistent with residential sorting by income and family type.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Married families compete for scarce suburban housing in high-income regions, which supports home prices there.
insights.quote: Many are located in high-income regions with limited housing availability, such as the San Francisco Bay Area and Northern Virginia.

insights.claim: Households with children make up 21% of all households on average in the top 10 US married-family deserts, compared with 44% in the top 10 married-family gardens, roughly twice as many.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Areas where married families dominate also have many more children, so demand for schools, child-related goods and family housing concentrates there.
insights.quote: On average, households with children account for 21% of all households in the top 10 married-family deserts, compared with 44% in the top 10 married-family gardens.

insights.claim: Among the top 10 US married-family deserts, the share of households with children ranges from 15% in a Detroit PUMA to 26% in western Chicago, while among the top gardens it ranges from 34% in Illinois's Northfield and New Trier Townships to 57% in western Utah County.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: The concentration of children varies widely by location, which matters for local school funding and demand for youth-oriented retail.

insights.claim: IFS Senior Fellow Lyman Stone finds that recent US fertility declines have been driven disproportionately by lower birth rates among unmarried and lower-income people, so births are increasingly concentrated among married, economically stable households.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: As births concentrate among married, higher-income households, demand for family-oriented goods shifts toward more affluent consumers.
insights.quote: recent declines in fertility have been driven disproportionately by lower birth rates among the unmarried and among lower-income populations

insights.claim: The IFS report says US married-family deserts increasingly function as adult-oriented or 'post-family' spaces, while married-family gardens are more conducive to having and raising children.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Urban cores may increasingly cater to adults (services, housing, amenities) while child-oriented spending moves to the suburbs.
insights.quote: Married-family deserts appear, on this evidence, to function increasingly as adult-oriented or post-family spaces

insights.claim: The IFS report says differences in family structure across US areas have implications for schools, housing markets, tax bases, welfare systems, local politics, and the balance between services for children and services for older people.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Local family structure is an input for municipal credit, school enrollment and real-estate demand forecasts.
insights.quote: These differences have implications for schools, housing markets, tax bases, welfare systems, local politics, and the balance between services oriented toward children and those oriented toward older populations.

insights.claim: Across all PUMAs, the overall marriage rate predicts the share of households with children better than the married-family share does, and the authors say housing availability, affordability and local institutions likely affect how strongly marriage translates into higher fertility.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Housing affordability may limit how much higher marriage rates raise local birth numbers.
insights.quote: additional factors—particularly housing availability, affordability, and local institutional capacity—are likely to shape how strongly marriage translates into higher fertility in different places
insights.locator: At the same time, these results

insights.claim: 'Double deserts', areas with both low adult marriage and few married-parent households, appear in parts of Atlanta, Baltimore, Chicago, Cleveland, Detroit, Los Angeles, Newark, New York, Philadelphia and Washington D.C.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: These neighborhoods face compounding disadvantage in family stability, which affects long-term demand for social services and local economic mobility.

insights.claim: In 'delayed-marriage deserts' such as parts of Manhattan, Brooklyn, Washington D.C., Los Angeles and college towns, adult marriage rates are low but a high share of parents are married, which suggests that young migrants marry late but before having children.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Low marriage rates in high-income job hubs may reflect delayed marriage rather than its absence, a different demographic profile from double deserts.
insights.quote: It is possible that, in these areas, young people remain single longer but ultimately get married prior to having children, provided that they remain in the area.

insights.claim: The IFS report warns that 'desert corridors' such as the Mississippi Delta and New Mexico, with below-average marriage and desert-level married-family shares, could become 'double deserts' in coming decades as children who grow up without married role models repeat those patterns.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Low-marriage regions risk falling further, with lower fertility, more single-parent households and weaker local tax bases.
insights.quote: These desert corridors, therefore, are vulnerable to becoming double deserts in the coming decades.

insights.claim: Rural areas such as central Appalachia (between West Virginia and Kentucky), central California and rural Nevada show above-average adult marriage rates but low shares of married-parent households, possibly because older adults married but their children are having children outside marriage.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Rural family decline may be generational and recent, so it could be easier to reverse than in areas where marriage was never the norm.
insights.quote: One possibility is that older adults in these regions generally chose to get married, but their adult children are having children without first getting married.
